## <span style="color: #69BA53;">Code of Conduct</span> {#CoC}

A psychologically safe and harassment-free working environment is pivotal to enable us to "**belong and be challenged**" together \@ref(belong) 

Harassment includes offensive verbal comments related to gender, gender identity and expression, age, sexual orientation, disability, socioecnomic status, physical appearance, body size, race, religion (or lack therof), sexual images in public spaces, deliberate intimidation, stalking, following, harassing photography or recording, sustained disruption of talks or other events, inappropriate physical contact, and unwelcome sexual attention.

Members asked to stop any harassing behavior are expected to comply immediately.

If you are being harassed, notice that someone else is being harassed, or have any other concerns, please contact Titus Brown immediately. If Titus is the cause of your concern, Cait Pickens (caitsydney at gmail.com) is a good informal point of contact; she does not work for Titus or UC Davis, and has agreed to mediate. For official concerns, please see the UC Davis ombuds office.

What is **a sense of belonging**?


What is **psychological safety**?
  
"*Psychological safety is defined as a "shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking". Such interpersonal risks include open communication, voicing concerns, asking questions and seeking feedback <u>without fear of judgment</u>. A psychologically safe environment allows all individuals to be their authentic selves and reduce work-related stress, leading to increased engagement and learning.*"

  * Citation: Hardie, P., O’Donovan, R., Jarvis, S., & Redmond, C. (2022). Key tips to providing a psychologically safe learning environment in the clinical setting. BMC Medical Education, 22(1), 816.

# <span style="color: #0066cc;">Lab philosophy</span> {#pedagogy}

---

## <span style="color: #69BA53;">About</span>

There are five interlocking pillars that define our philosophy: 
  
  (1) Belong to be challenged
  
  (2) Reciprocal expectations
  
  (3) Structured skill development
  
  (4) Rigorous, ethical research practice
  
  (5) Continuous reflection and feedback, for both mentor and mentee(s)

### <span style="color: #CFC22B;">Belong to be challenged</span> {#belong}

Refer to the lab Code of Conduct \@ref(pedagogy)

The leader’s first responsibility is to cultivate a psychologically healthy research environment where mentees can give, receive, and act on feedback without fear of personal attack, retaliation, or humiliation. This includes explicitly normalizing that everyone makes mistakes, treating lapses as opportunities to learn, and addressing uncivil or insensitive behavior through calm, non defensive conversations that focus on patterns rather than isolated incidents.
A humanistic approach emphasizes respect and compassion for every lab member regardless of career stage, background, or role, recognizing that people bring diverse histories and tolerance levels for incivility to work. The mentor sets the tone by modeling dignity and respect in all interactions and by ensuring a safe and supportive environment free from harassment and discrimination, consistent with institutional policies and mandatory reporting obligations.

### <span style="color: #CFC22B;">Explicit, reciprocal expectations</span>

Effective mentorship is framed as a mutual agreement with clearly articulated expectations in both directions, ideally documented in a living “lab expectations” or advisor–advisee agreement co revised over time. The mentor should specify expectations around honesty, communication, lab presence, participation in lab community, authorship discussion, and contribution to shared lab responsibilities, while also stating what trainees can reliably expect from the mentor (regular meetings, timely feedback, advocacy, networking, letters, and help planning timelines and funding).
The pedagogy stresses that mentees are responsible for their own careers: they should actively seek advice, critically evaluate it, and take ownership of scientific direction within the broad themes of the lab, including raising concerns, setting boundaries, and considering lab changes if interests diverge. Regular one on one check ins and explicit conversation about meeting frequency, workload, attention, and perceived inequities help prevent isolation, misaligned expectations, and resentment among trainees.


### <span style="color: #CFC22B;">Structured skill and career development</span>

Mentorship is not limited to data or manuscripts; it encompasses systematic development of research, communication, and leadership skills across career stages. The mentor intentionally trains mentees in study design, power analysis, lab notebook practice, sample management, solution preparation, and data management, using SOPs and templates to scaffold good habits and reproducible work.
Professional development includes guiding course choices, conference participation, grant writing, and outreach, and encouraging mentees to pursue independent ideas that align with lab themes while learning to “sell” those ideas through proposals and presentations. A core expectation is that more senior mentees practice mentoring themselves (e.g., by supervising undergraduates), with the PI supporting this as both a training experience and a way to propagate healthy mentoring practices through the group.

### <span style="color: #CFC22B;">Rigorous, ethical research practice</span>

The pedagogy embeds responsible conduct of research and research integrity into routine lab life rather than treating them as one off trainings. This includes explicit instruction and ongoing discussion about scientific rigor (reproducibility, accurate record keeping, appropriate statistics, data normalization and outlier handling), as well as authorship norms, avoidance of gift/ghost authorship, and appropriate credit through authorship or acknowledgments based on material and intellectual contribution.

Mentors ensure all lab members complete required RCR and safety trainings, understand ethical and regulatory expectations (human/animal subjects, biosafety, data confidentiality, conflicts of interest), and follow clear policies for data ownership, sharing, and handling during lab transitions and departures. The PI is framed as custodian of data and culture, responsible for aligning lab practices with institutional policies and disciplinary codes of ethics while modeling transparent, accountable behavior.

### <span style="color: #CFC22B;">Continuous reflection, feedback, and growth</span>

A central tenet is a growth mindset for both mentor and mentees, grounded in ongoing reflection and willingness to seek advice, adapt, and improve communication and leadership skills. The mentor regularly invites candid feedback about the lab climate and their own mentoring, treats criticism as valuable data, and, when missteps occur, de escalates, acknowledges impact, and works with mentees to decide how to move forward constructively.
Mentees are encouraged to self assess strengths and areas for development, to signal when they need more structure or support, and to build a broader mentoring network beyond the primary PI. Throughout, the pedagogy positions mentorship as a collaborative, evolving relationship in which mentor and mentees co create a respectful, rigorous, and inclusive research community that supports both excellent science and sustainable, humane careers.

## math example

$p$ is unknown but expected to be around 1/3. Standard error will be approximated

$$
SE = \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}} \approx \sqrt{\frac{1/3 (1 - 1/3)} {300}} = 0.027
$$
